newsitem.title: JAPAN: THAI CREDITOR MEETING OPENS IN TOKYO.
newsitem.headline: THAI CREDITOR MEETING OPENS IN TOKYO.

text.p: A meeting of creditors opened in Tokyo on Monday to discuss a loan package to help ease Thailand's financial crisis.

Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya, who said on Sunday he needed at least $10 billion in standby credit from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other lenders, declined to comment as he went into the conference.
Participating in the meeting are 13 countries and three multilateral financial institutions -- the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.
An IMF official said some of the countries were attending as observers, but he said the breakdown of which ones were observers was unclear and would be decided during the meeting.
He said that it was possible observer nations will not contribute money to an overall Thai rescue package.

The IMF official, based in Tokyo, said: "The meeting is not just something to approve an IMF programme for Thailand. I am sure there will be an explanation about the programme to the participants and they will discuss how much each country can support Thailand."
An IMF spokesman said he had not heard whether IMF representatives would meet with Japanese private-sector banks.

The morning session is to continue until 1.00 p.m. (0400 GMT). Thanong is to meet Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka at 1.30 p.m. (0430 GMT), after which the two ministers are due to hold a news conference at 2.00 p.m. (0500 GMT).

The afternoon session will be from 2.30 p.m. (0530 GMT) until 4.00 p.m. (0700 GMT), followed by a joint news conference at 4.30 p.m. (0730 GMT) by IMF Deputy Managing Director Shigemitsu Sugisaki, Japanese Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs Eisuke Sakakibara and a Thai representative.

Thailand, in deep recession as a result of the collapse of a real estate and asset "bubble", announced on August 5 a series of economic reform measures and said it was seeking the loans from foreign countries and the IMF to stabilise its economy.

The measures it took included suspension of more than half of the finance companies operating in Thailand, a three percentage point rise in the value-added tax and strict monetary and fiscal targets for the next few years.

Japanese officials have said the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) were likely to take part in the rescue effort, but that the bulk of financial support would come from the IMF and Japan.
Japanese officials say Tokyo's contribution will be almost totally in the form of untied loans through the government-run Export-Import Bank of Japan.

In addition to the government support, private Japanese banks are expected to provide several billion dollars, given their heavy loan exposure in Thailand and the hefty direct investment by Japanese firms.
Thailand has nearly $90 billion in foreign currency debt and Japanese bankers estimate about $36 billion of that is owed to Japanese banks.
Thanong said on Sunday that most of the discussions would be held with countries in the Asian region. He said the programme in Japan was arranged by the IMF and not by Thailand.
Thailand is a member of the Association of South East Nations (ASEAN), which also includes the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore, Vietnam, Brunei, Burma, Laos and Malaysia.
Thai Finance Ministry sources have said Singapore is the only likely lender from ASEAN.

Other sources said Thailand was likely to borrow from $12 to $15 billion, with $7 billion from Japan's Export-Import Bank, $4 billion from the IMF, $1 billion from the World Bank, $1 billion from the Asia Development Bank, and the rest from other sources.
They said the United States could also support the IMF package once a recovery programme was worked out.
A Thanong aide told Reuters that the finance minister may meet leading figures of Japan's private sector on Tuesday before returning to Thailand later that day.
More than 40 percent of Thailand's estimated $90 billion in foreign currency debt is short-term.
The problem has been exacerbated by a crisis of confidence that has left foreign creditors and investors reluctant to pour in much-needed funds, resulting in severe liquidity problems.

In last week's fiscal and monetary measures to put the country back on track, the Thai government vowed to balance the budget, maintain at least $25 billion in foreign reserves, resolve financial sector ills, cut government risk exposure to the financial sector, maintain a tight monetary policy and cap annual inflation at eight to nine percent.
